facts.statement: The front of the lower jaw of Giganotosaurus was flattened and had a downward-projecting process at the tip.
facts.quote: The front of the lower jaw was flattened and had a downward-projecting process (or "chin") at the tip.

facts.statement: The teeth of Giganotosaurus were compressed sideways and had serrations.

facts.statement: Giganotosaurus had a strong neck and a proportionally small pectoral girdle.

facts.statement: Giganotosaurus is thought to have been homeothermic with a metabolism between that of a mammal and a reptile, enabling fast growth.
facts.quote: Giganotosaurus is thought to have been homeothermic (a type of "warm-bloodedness"), with a metabolism between that of a mammal and a reptile, which would have enabled fast growth.

facts.statement: Giganotosaurus was capable of closing its jaws quickly to capture prey by delivering powerful bites.
facts.quote: It would have been capable of closing its jaws quickly, capturing and bringing down prey by delivering powerful bites.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the "chin" of Giganotosaurus may have helped resist stress when delivering a bite against prey.
facts.quote: The "chin" may have helped in resisting stress when a bite was delivered against prey.

facts.statement: In 1993, amateur fossil hunter Rubén Darío Carolini discovered a theropod tibia while driving near Villa El Chocón in Neuquén province, Argentina.
facts.quote: In 1993, the amateur Argentine fossil hunter Rubén Darío Carolini discovered the tibia (lower leg bone) of a theropod dinosaur while driving a dune buggy in the badlands near Villa El Chocón, in the Neuquén province of Patagonia, Argentina.

facts.statement: The discovery was announced by paleontologists Rodolfo Coria and Leonardo Salgado at a Society of Vertebrate Paleontology meeting in 1994.
facts.quote: The discovery was announced by the paleontologists Rodolfo Coria and Leonardo Salgado at a Society of Vertebrate Paleontology meeting in 1994

facts.statement: The holotype specimen preserved almost 70% of the skeleton.
facts.quote: The specimen preserved almost 70% of the skeleton

facts.statement: The holotype skeleton is housed in the Ernesto Bachmann Paleontological Museum in Villa El Chocón, catalogued as specimen MUCPv-Ch1.
facts.quote: The holotype skeleton is now housed in the Ernesto Bachmann Paleontological Museum (where it is catalogued as specimen MUCPv-Ch1) in Villa El Chocón

facts.statement: The generic name Giganotosaurus is derived from Ancient Greek words meaning "giant," "southern," and "lizard."
facts.quote: The generic name is derived from the Ancient Greek words gigas/ (meaning "giant"), notos/ (meaning "austral/southern", in reference to its provenance) and -sauros/- (meaning "lizard").

facts.statement: It is debated whether Giganotosaurus was larger than Tyrannosaurus, roughly equal in size, or if its largest size estimates are exaggerated.
facts.quote: Some researchers have found the animal to be larger than Tyrannosaurus, which has historically been considered the largest theropod, while others have found them to be roughly equal in size and the largest size estimates for Giganotosaurus exaggerated.

facts.statement: The first known fossil of Giganotosaurus is an incomplete tooth discovered near Lake Ezequiel Ramos Mexia in 1987 by A. Delgado.
facts.quote: In 1999, Calvo assigned an incomplete tooth, (MUCPv-52), to Giganotosaurus; this specimen was discovered near Lake Ezequiel Ramos Mexia in 1987 by A. Delgado, and is therefore the first known fossil of the genus.

facts.statement: Tracks attributed to Giganotosaurus range from 36 cm to 50 cm in length with paces between 100 cm and 130 cm.
facts.quote: The largest tracks are 50 cm long with a pace of 130 cm, and the smallest is 36 cm long with a pace of 100 cm.

facts.statement: The tracks attributed to Giganotosaurus are three-toed with large, coarse digits and prominent claw impressions.
facts.quote: The tracks are tridactyl (three-toed) and have large and coarse digits, with prominent claw impressions.

facts.statement: In 2001, Frank Seebacher estimated Giganotosaurus weighed 6.6 metric tons based on a 12.5-meter length.
facts.quote: In 2001, the physician-scientist Frank Seebacher proposed a new polynomial method of calculating body-mass estimates for dinosaurs (using body-length, depth, and width), and found Giganotosaurus to have weighed 6.6 MT (based on the original 12.5 m length estimate).

facts.statement: In 2002, Coria and Currie estimated the Giganotosaurus holotype skull was 1.60 meters long and the animal weighed 4.2 metric tons.
facts.quote: In their 2002 description of the braincase of Giganotosaurus, Coria and Currie gave a length estimate of 1.60 m for the holotype skull, and calculated a weight of 4.2 MT by extrapolating from the 520 mm circumference of the femur-shaft.

facts.statement: In 2004, Mazzetta and colleagues noted the Giganotosaurus holotype tibia was 1.12 meters long, 8 cm shorter than that of 'Sue'.
facts.quote: In 2004, the paleontologist Gerardo V. Mazzetta and colleagues pointed out that though the femur of the Giganotosaurus holotype was larger than that of "Sue", the tibia was 8 cm shorter at 1.12 m.

facts.statement: Mazzetta and colleagues suggested the Giganotosaurus holotype weighed 8 metric tons, while a larger specimen with a bigger dentary could have weighed 10 metric tons.
facts.quote: They found the holotype specimen to have been equal to Tyrannosaurus in size at 8 MT (marginally smaller than "Sue"), but that the larger dentary might have represented an animal of 10 MT, if geometrically similar to the holotype specimen.

facts.statement: Therrien and Henderson revised Spinosaurus estimates to 14.3 meters and 20.9 metric tons, or alternatively 12.6 meters and 12 metric tons.
facts.quote: They also found that Dal Sasso and colleagues' reconstruction of Spinosaurus was too large, and instead estimated it to have been 14.3 m long, weighing 20.9 MT, and possibly as low as 12.6 m in length and 12 MT in weight.

facts.statement: In 2012, Carrano and colleagues noted that the Giganotosaurus holotype had not been described in detail beyond the braincase.
facts.quote: In 2012, the paleontologist Matthew T. Carrano and colleagues noted that though Giganotosaurus had received much attention due to its enormous size, and in spite of the holotype being relatively complete, it had not yet been described in detail, apart from the braincase.

facts.statement: Carrano and colleagues found the skulls of Giganotosaurus and Carcharodontosaurus were the same size as that of Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: They found instead that the skulls of Giganotosaurus and Carcharodontosaurus were exactly the same size as that of Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2013, Scott Hartman estimated Tyrannosaurus was larger overall than Giganotosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2013, the paleontologist Scott Hartman published a Graphic Double Integration mass estimate (based on drawn skeletal reconstructions) on his blog, wherein he found Tyrannosaurus ("Sue") to have been larger than Giganotosaurus overall.

facts.statement: Scott Hartman estimated the Giganotosaurus holotype weighed 6.8 metric tons and a larger specimen weighed 8.2 metric tons.
facts.quote: He estimated the Giganotosaurus holotype to have weighed 6.8 MT, and the larger specimen 8.2 MT.

facts.statement: In 2021, Reolid and colleagues excluded Therrien and Henderson's 2007 estimates when calculating average theropod mass, considering them outliers.
facts.quote: In 2021, the paleontologist Matías Reolid and colleagues compiled various mass estimates of theropods (including Giganotosaurus) to calculate the average, but did not include Therrien and Henderson's 2007 estimates of Carnotaurus and Giganotosaurus, considering them outliers.

facts.statement: Reolid and colleagues estimated a 13-meter-long Giganotosaurus could weigh up to 7.2 metric tons using 3D models.
facts.quote: They also applied the skull length and body length ratio proposed by Therrien and Henderson and reconstructed various digital 3D models of theropods to measure body mass distribution and volume, resulting in the mass of a 13 m long Giganotosaurus up to 7.2 MT.

facts.statement: In 2022, Canale and colleagues described Meraxes, which has the most complete Carcharodontosaurine skull at an estimated 1.27 meters long.
facts.quote: In 2022, Juan I. Canale and colleagues described the large carcharodontosaurid Meraxes, which has the most completely known Carcharodontosaurine skull, with an estimated length of 1.27 m.

facts.statement: In 2023, Henderson suggested pelvic dimensions correlate with body size in theropods, allowing estimates for incomplete specimens.
facts.quote: Henderson suggested in 2023 that there was a close relation between the dimensions of the pelvic area and body size in theropods, allowing size estimates for incomplete specimens.

facts.statement: Using pelvic dimensions, Henderson estimated Giganotosaurus was 12.5 meters long, matching the 1995 description.
facts.quote: Based on this idea, he found Giganotosaurus to have been 12.5 m long, identical to the estimate proposed in the 1995 description.

facts.statement: Giganotosaurus is considered one of the largest theropod dinosaurs, though its incomplete remains make reliable size estimates difficult.
facts.quote: Giganotosaurus is thought to have been one of the largest theropod dinosaurs, but the incompleteness of its remains have made it difficult to estimate its size reliably.

facts.statement: Estimates for the holotype specimen suggest a length of 12 to 13 meters, a skull length of 1.53 to 1.80 meters, a femur length of 1.365 to 1.43 meters, and a weight of 4.2 to 13.8 metric tons.
facts.quote: Length estimates for the holotype specimen have varied between 12 and 13 m, with a skull between 1.53 and 1.80 m long, a femur (thigh bone) between 1.365 and 1.43 m long, and a weight between 4.2 and 13.8 MT.

facts.statement: Fusion of sutures in the braincase indicates that the holotype specimen was a mature individual.
facts.quote: Fusion of sutures (joints) in the braincase indicates the holotype specimen was a mature individual.

facts.statement: The maxilla of the upper jaw had a tooth row 92 centimeters long, was deep from top to bottom, and had almost parallel upper and lower edges.
facts.quote: The maxilla of the upper jaw had a 92 cm long tooth row, was deep from top to bottom, and its upper and lower edges were almost parallel.

facts.statement: The nasal bone was very rugose, with roughness covering its entire upper surface.
facts.quote: The nasal bone was very rugose (rough and wrinkled), and these rugosities continued backwards, covering the entire upper surface of this bone.

facts.statement: The lacrimal crest was ridge-like and featured deep grooves.
facts.quote: The crest was ridge-like, and had deep grooves.

facts.statement: The jaw of Giganotosaurus articulated far behind the occipital condyle compared to other theropods.
facts.quote: The jaw articulated far behind the occipital condyle (where the neck is attached to the skull) compared to other theropods.

facts.statement: A latex endocast of the brain cavity showed that the brain of Giganotosaurus was similar to that of Carcharodontosaurus but larger.
facts.quote: A latex endocast of the brain cavity of Giganotosaurus showed that the brain was similar to that of the related genus Carcharodontosaurus, but larger.

facts.statement: The brain endocast was 29 millimeters long, 64 millimeters wide, and had a volume of 275 milliliters.
facts.quote: The endocast was 29 mm long, 64 mm wide, and had a volume of 275 ml.

facts.statement: It is possible that each dentary of Giganotosaurus had twelve alveoli.
facts.quote: It is possible that each dentary had twelve alveoli.

facts.statement: Most of the alveoli were about 3.5 centimeters long from front to back.
facts.quote: Most of the alveoli were about 3.5 cm (1.3 in) long from front to back.

facts.statement: The neck of Giganotosaurus was strong, and the axis bone was robust.
facts.quote: The neck of Giganotosaurus was strong, and the axis bone (the neck vertebra that articulates with the skull) was robust.

facts.statement: The ischium was straight, expanded hindwards, and ended in a lobe-shape.
facts.quote: The ischium was straight and expanded hindwards, ending in a lobe-shape.

facts.statement: The femur was sigmoid-shaped with a very robust, upward-pointing head and a deep sulcus.
facts.quote: The femur was sigmoid-shaped, and had a very robust, upwards pointing head, with a deep sulcus (groove).

facts.statement: The fourth trochanter of the femur was large and projected backwards.
facts.quote: The fourth trochanter was large and projected backwards.

facts.statement: Other features indicated that Giganotosaurus was outside the derived clade Coelurosauria.
facts.quote: Other features showed that it was outside the more derived (or "advanced") clade Coelurosauria.

facts.statement: In 1996, Sereno and colleagues grouped Giganotosaurus, Carcharodontosaurus, and Acrocanthosaurus within the superfamily Allosauroidea and the family Carcharodontosauridae.
facts.quote: In 1996, Sereno and colleagues found Giganotosaurus, Carcharodontosaurus, and Acrocanthosaurus to be closely related within the superfamily Allosauroidea, and grouped them in the family Carcharodontosauridae.

facts.statement: In 2004, Thomas R. Holtz and colleagues defined the family Carcharodontosauridae as all allosauroids closer to Carcharodontosaurus than to Allosaurus or Sinraptor.
facts.quote: The group was defined as all allosauroids closer to Carcharodontosaurus than Allosaurus or Sinraptor by the paleontologist Thomas R. Holtz and colleagues in 2004.

facts.statement: In 2008, Sereno and Stephen L. Brusatte united Giganotosaurus, Mapusaurus, and Tyrannotitan in the tribe Giganotosaurini.
facts.quote: In 2008, Sereno and the paleontologist Stephen L. Brusatte united Giganotosaurus, Mapusaurus, and Tyrannotitan in the tribe Giganotosaurini.

facts.statement: In 2010, Paul listed Giganotosaurus as "Giganotosaurus (or Carcharodontosaurus) carolinii" without elaboration.
facts.quote: In 2010, Paul listed Giganotosaurus as "Giganotosaurus (or Carcharodontosaurus) carolinii" without elaboration.

facts.statement: It is impossible to determine with certainty whether Giganotosaurus was larger than Tyrannosaurus, which has historically been considered the largest theropod.
facts.quote: It is therefore impossible to determine with certainty whether it was larger than Tyrannosaurus, for example, which has been considered the largest theropod historically.

facts.statement: The name Giganotosaurus carolinii includes 'carolinii' to honor its discoverer.
facts.quote: su descubridor

facts.statement: Giganotosaurus lived between 99 and 95 million years ago during the Cenomanian stage of the Early Cretaceous in what is now Patagonia, Argentina.
facts.quote: que vivió hace entre 99 a 95 millones de años, en el Cenomaniano (inicios de la época Cretácico Inferior). en lo que hoy es la Patagonia Argentina.

facts.statement: Giganotosaurus likely used its keen sense of smell for tracking and its large jaws with long, flattened, serrated teeth for cutting and tearing flesh.
facts.quote: Tenía como herramienta de rastreo su agudo olfato y como principal arma de ataque sus grandes fauces dotadas de largos y achatados dientes con bordes dentados, especializados para cortar y desgarrar profundamente la carne de sus víctimas.

facts.statement: Based on the holotype specimen MUCPv-CH-1, studies estimate Giganotosaurus to be 12 to 13 meters long, weigh between 6.1 and 6.9 tons, and stand over 4 meters tall at the hips.
facts.quote: Basándose en el holotipo, MUCPv-CH-1, diferentes estudios a lo largo de los años han estimado al Giganotosaurus en un rango de entre 12 y 13 m de longitud, de 6,1 a 6,9 tn de peso, y con una altura superior a unos 4 m hasta las caderas.

facts.statement: The skull length of Giganotosaurus was originally estimated at 1.8 meters but is now corrected to 1.56 meters.
facts.quote: La longitud del cráneo fue originalmente estimada en 1,8 m pero se ha demostrado que esta reconstrucción es errónea y actualmente se estima en 1,56 m.

facts.statement: The femur of Giganotosaurus measures up to 143 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: El fémur, o hueso del muslo, mide hasta 143 cm de largo.

facts.statement: Giganotosaurus was a bipedal predator with a large skull supported by a powerful neck, short forelimbs with three curved claws, and powerful hind limbs.
facts.quote: El Giganotosaurus era un depredador bípedo con un gran cráneo sostenido por un cuello poderoso, extremidades superiores cortas en proporción a su tamaño, provistas de tres dedos terminados en garras curvas y afiladas, y extremidades inferiores poderosas.

facts.statement: Giganotosaurus likely preyed on a wide range of saurischians, including giant titanosaur sauropods.
facts.quote: Es probable que haya depredado una amplia gama de animales saurópsidos, incluyendo hasta gigantescos saurópodos titanosaurianos.

facts.statement: Giganotosaurus was possibly a homeothermic organism with an active lifestyle and faster growth than cold-blooded reptiles.
facts.quote: Posiblemente se haya tratado de un organismo homeotermo y, por lo tanto, un animal con un estilo de vida activo y de crecimiento más rápido que un reptil de sangre fría.

facts.statement: Giganotosaurus had a femur longer than its tibia, indicating its legs provided strong support but not high speed.
facts.quote: Las patas posteriores del Giganotosaurus se caracterizaban por tener un fémur más largo que la tibia, lo que indica que sus piernas lo dotaban de gran soporte pero no de gran velocidad.

facts.statement: The leg proportions of Giganotosaurus suggest it was an ambush predator or hunted slow prey like sauropods.
facts.quote: Esto sugiere que era un depredador de emboscada o que cazaba presas lentas, como los saurópodos.

facts.statement: Research by Sereno and colleagues indicates that carcharodontosaurids had a transcontinental distribution by the Early Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Sereno and colleagues found that the presence of carcharodontosaurids in Africa (Carcharodontosaurus), North America (Acrocanthosaurus), and South America (Giganotosaurus), showed the group had a transcontinental distribution by the Early Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: In 1999 and 2002, Reese E. Barrick and William J. Showers found that Giganotosaurus and Tyrannosaurus had similar oxygen isotope patterns and body heat distribution.
facts.quote: In 1999 and 2002, the paleontologist Reese E. Barrick and the geologist William J. Showers found that the bones of Giganotosaurus and Tyrannosaurus had very similar oxygen isotope patterns, with similar heat distribution in the body.

facts.statement: Thermoregulatory patterns suggest Giganotosaurus had a metabolism intermediate between mammals and reptiles, making it homeothermic.
facts.quote: These thermoregulatory patterns indicate that these dinosaurs had a metabolism intermediate between that of mammals and reptiles, and were therefore homeothermic (with a stable core body-temperature, a type of "warm-bloodedness").

facts.statement: An 8-ton Giganotosaurus would have had a metabolism comparable to a 1-ton mammalian carnivore, supporting rapid growth.
facts.quote: The metabolism of an 8 MT Giganotosaurus would be comparable to that of a 1 MT mammalian carnivore, and would have supported rapid growth.

facts.statement: In 2001, Rudemar Ernesto Blanco and Mazzetta evaluated the running capability of Giganotosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2001, the physicist Rudemar Ernesto Blanco and Mazzetta evaluated the cursorial (running) capability of Giganotosaurus.

facts.statement: Blanco and Mazzetta calculated that the upper kinematic limit of Giganotosaurus running speed was 14 meters per second.
facts.quote: Calculating the time it would take for a leg to gain balance after the retraction of the opposite leg, they found the upper kinematic limit of the running speed to be 14 m/s.

facts.statement: Comparisons between Giganotosaurus running capability and birds like ostriches based on leg-bone strength are of limited value because theropods had heavy tails for balance.
facts.quote: They also found comparison between the running capability of Giganotosaurus and birds like the ostrich based on the strength of their leg-bones to be of limited value, since theropods, unlike birds, had heavy tails to counterbalance their weight.

facts.statement: The size of Giganotosaurus is part of an intense scientific debate regarding the maximum sizes theropod dinosaurs can reach.
facts.quote: convirtiéndose en parte de un intenso debate científico acerca los tamaños máximos que pueden alcanzar los dinosaurios terópodos.

facts.statement: Giganotosaurus had the tallest hind legs of any theropod.
facts.quote: El Giganotosaurus contaba con unas de las extremidades posteriores, las piernas, más altas entre los terópodos.

facts.statement: In the holotype, the femur measured between 143 and 136.5 cm long, the tibia 112 cm, and the fibula about 84 cm.
facts.quote: En el holotipo, solo el fémur medía entre 143 y 136,5 cm de largo, la tibia medía 112 cm y el peroné unos 84 cm.

facts.statement: The femoral head had a sigmoid curve shape and was thicker than the rest of the bone.
facts.quote: La cabeza del fémur tenía forma de curva sigmoidea y estaba más engrosada que el resto del hueso.

facts.statement: It likely had forelimbs typical of a carnivorous theropod, relatively small compared to its body, with three fingers each ending in sharp claws.
facts.quote: Probablemente, presentaba las extremidades anteriores, brazos, de un terópodo carnosaurio típico, algo pequeñas en relación con su cuerpo, con tres dedos cada una, terminadas en afiladas garras.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the forelimbs may have been used as tools to hold prey while it was killed with its jaws.
facts.quote: Estas pudieron haberle servido como herramienta para sostener a sus presas mientras las mataba con su mandíbula.

facts.statement: The spine consisted of nine cervical vertebrae, fourteen dorsal vertebrae, five sacral vertebrae, and more than forty caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: La columna vertebral tenía un total de nueve vértebras cervicales, catorce vértebras dorsales, cinco vértebras sacras y más de cuarenta vértebras caudales.

facts.statement: The short, robust neck formed a less marked natural curve than in other theropods, with the typical S-shape almost non-existent.
facts.quote: El cuello, corto y robusto, formaba una curva natural menos marcada que en los demás terópodos, con la típica forma de S casi inexistente.

facts.statement: The characteristic neural spines caused the back to be straighter than most theropods and less arched than in Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: La forma característica de las espinas neurales del Giganotosaurus provocaba que su espalda fuese más recta que las de la mayoría de los terópodos, menos arqueada que en el caso de Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: The robust ribs formed an oval-shaped thoracic cage in frontal view, more robust than in other carcharodontosaurids but thinner than in tyrannosaurids.
facts.quote: Las costillas eran robustas y construían una caja torácica ovalada en vista frontal, más corpulenta que en los otros carcarodontosáuridos, pero más delgada que en los tiranosáuridos.

facts.quote: Parent group: Carcharodontosauridae
